title: Dennis Ritchie and the Creation of C at Bell Labs (1972)
explainer: C exists because Dennis Ritchie, working at Bell Labs, needed a language to rewrite the Unix operating system in — he built it in 1972 by extending an earlier, typeless language called B (itself derived from BCPL) with real data types and structures. That Unix-rewriting origin explains why C gives you direct, unmediated access to memory addresses through pointers rather than hiding them behind a safer abstraction: the language was designed for systems programmers who needed that control, not for application programmers who'd rather not think about it.

title: The Morris Worm and the First Internet-Scale Buffer Overflow (1988)
explainer: The pointer bugs this lesson warns about aren't just a classroom hazard: in November 1988, the Morris worm spread across a large share of the early internet partly by exploiting a stack buffer overflow in a Unix program called fingerd, which used an unbounded C function to copy input into a fixed-size buffer. It's considered one of the first buffer-overflow exploits used in the wild, and the incident is a direct, real-world instance of the exact failure mode this module's uninitialized-pointer and array-bounds warnings exist to prevent.
